documentation.range:
Chlorocebus pygerythrus is distributed from the Ethiopian Highlands (east of the Rift Valley) and southern Somalia in the north, through Kenya (including the Lamu Archipelago), eastern and southern Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania (including Pemba, Zanzibar, and Mafia Islands), Zambia (east of the Luangwa Valley), Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, northern and eastern Botswana, much of South Africa (all provinces), Eswatini, Lesotho, and southern Namibia (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Wallis 2013). Broadly sympatric with Papio spp. and Erythrocebus patas (T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2024). Present from sea level to at least 2,140 m (Mount Hanang, Tanzania; Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2009).

Six subspecies are recognised:

Chlorocebus pygerythrus arenaria (northeastern vervet; not arenarius as often used) occurs in the Ethiopian Highlands east of the Rift Valley, southern Somalia, the northern half of Kenya reaching beyond the Galana River (Tsavo) in the east and to Mount Elgon in the west, northeastern Uganda, and extreme southeastern South Sudan. Geographic range roughly 580,000 km². Altitudinal range 30–1,960 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022, De Jong and Butynski 2023).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus centralis (eastern vervet) occupies the southern Somalia coast south of the Shebelle River, coastal Kenya (including the Lamu Archipelago), southern Kenya, southern Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, all of Tanzania (including Unguja Island and Mafia Island) as far south as the Rufiji River and southern ends both of Lake Rukwa and Lake Tanganyika, and northwestern shore of Lake Tanganyika perhaps as far south as the Lukuga River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Butynski and De Jong 2022, De Jong and Butynski 2023). Western limit in Kenya and Uganda, relative to tantalus Chlorocebus tantalus (Ogilby, 1841) is poorly understood (Butynski and De Jong 2014, 2017; De Jong and Butynski 2014), as is the northern limit in northwestern Kenya, southeastern South Sudan, and northern Uganda relative to grivet Chlorocebus aethiops (De Jong and Butynski 2014). Geographic range roughly 1,064,000 km². Altitudinal range 0–2,140 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022, De Jong and Butynski 2023).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus nesiotes (Pemba vervet) is endemic to Pemba Island, off the north coast of Tanzania (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013). Geographic range <988 km². Altitudinal range 0–95 m asl (De Jong and Butynski 2023).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus pygerythrus (southern vervet) occurs south of the Zambezi River from the Okavango Delta in northwestern Botswana, through Zimbabwe, southern Mozambique, South Africa, Eswatini, Lesotho, and extreme southern Namibia (Skinner and Chimimba 2005, Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Turner et al. 2016). Its western limit, relative to Chlorocebus cynosures, is poorly understood but appears to be in northwestern Botswana (Smithers 1971, Sarmiento 2013). Altitudinal range from 0–1,525 m asl (T. Turner pers. comm.).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus rufoviridis (reddish-green vervet) ranges south of the Rufiji River and Lake Rukwa in southern Tanzania southward through Malawi, northern Mozambique, and eastern Zambia to the Zambezi River east of the Luangwa River. Perhaps on the western side of Lake Tanganyika northward to at least the Lukugu River, Democratic Republic of Congo. Geographic range roughly 885,000 km². Altitudinal range 0–1,900 m asl (De Jong and Butynski 2023).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus zavattarii (Omo vervet) occurs in southwestern Ethiopia and central north Kenya, between the northern end of Lake Turkana and the southern end of Lake Abaya. Geographic distribution is poorly understood. Geographic range roughly 34,000 km². Altitudinal range 400–1,500 m asl (Butynski and De Jong 2022, Y. de Jong and T. Butynski unpubl. data).
documentation.population: Chlorocebus pygerythrus is patchily distributed over its extensive geographic range, probably due to the need to drink water daily and for large trees in which to sleep (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2024). Densities vary between 9 and 104 individuals/km² (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013). Locally abundant but there are large areas within the geographic range from which it is absent. In cultivated areas and at tourist sites, it is often regarded as a nuisance due to raiding (Y. de Jong and T. Butynski pers. obs. 2024). Small, isolated, populations may be prone to local extinction (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013).
documentation.habitats: Chlorocebus pygerythrus is a medium-sized, semi-terrestrial primate which occupies savanna, open woodland, and forest-grassland mosaic, especially close to rivers and lake shores. Adaptable and able to persist in secondary and/or highly fragmented habitats, including cultivated areas, and often found in rural and urban environments. A significant part of the range consists of miombo woodland. Chlorocebus pygerythrus is typically absent from deserts and deep forest. Lives in multi-male/multi-female groups of up to 38 individuals; many unrelated males may be present in a group. Home ranges vary from 5 to 103 ha. Chlorocebus pygerythrus sleeps in tall trees and is omnivorous, feeding on gum, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, and invertebrates (Skinner and Chimimba 2005, Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Wallis 2013, Turner et al. 2016).
documentation.threats:
Although C. pygerythrus is adaptable and widespread, the very patchy distribution and often small populations make it vulnerable to local decline or extinction. The main threats to this species are human-caused habitat degradation, fragmentation, and loss (De Jong and Butynski 2009, Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Wallis 2013).

Chlorocebus pygerythrus is often considered a nuisance. It is persecuted in response to crop raiding or negative interactions at tourist facilities (Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013, Wallis 2013, Turner et al. 2016, T. Butynski and Y. de Jong pers. obs. 2024). This monkey is a source of bushmeat in some areas (Turner et al. 2016), including Turkana District, Kenya (de Jong et al. 2008).
documentation.measures:
Chlorocebus pygerythrus is listed on Appendix II of CITES and on Class B of the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. 

Further taxonomic work is required to assess the validity C. pygerythrus as a species and of the currently recognised six subspecies.

Present in many protected areas throughout its range.

Prevention of crop raiding and negative interactions at tourist facilities is essential to avoid further escalation of human-non-human primate conflicts and the transmission of diseases.
documentation.use_trade: This species is a source of bushmeat in some areas, including Turkana District, Kenya (De Jong et al. 2008).
documentation.rationale: Vervet Chlorocebus pygerythrus is assessed as Least Concern. This species has a wide, albeit much fragmented, geographic range in which it is locally abundant. Although C. pygerythrus is in decline overall, there is no evidence of a significant range-wide population decline that would warrant listing in a higher category of threat.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Napier (1981) and Grubb et al. (2003) considered the Vervet monkey to be a subspecies of Grivet Cercopithecus aethiops (Linnaeus, 1758). Here the Vervet is treated as a species following Hill (1966), Dandelot (1974), Kingdon (1997, 2015), Groves (2001, 2005), Groves and Kingdon (2013), Isbell and Jaffe (2013), and Wallis (2013), and placed in the genus Chlorocebus Gray, 1870, following Groves (1989, 2001, 2005), Groves and Kingdon (2013), Isbell and Enstam Jaffe (2013), Wallis (2013), and Kingdon (2015).

De Jong and Butynski (2024) examined the hilgerti Neumann, 1902 holotype and three paratypes at the Museum für Naturkunde, Berlin and concluded that hilgerti is not a Vervet Chlorocebus pygerythrus (F. Cuvier, 1821) (as per Groves 2001, 2005; Grubb et al. 2003; Haus et al. 2013; Isbell and Enstam Jaffe 2013; Wallis 2013), but rather a Grivet C.  aethiops.

The Omo vervet C. p. zavattarii (de Beaux, 1943) was originally described as a Grivet, but is now considered to be a Vervet (Dandelot 1974; Grubb et al. 2003; Butynski and De Jong 2022).

Following Groves (2001), Grubb et al. (2003), Isbell and Enstam Jaffe (2013), and De Jong and Butynski (2023), the Manda Vervet C. p. excubitor (Schwarz, 1926) is not recognized as the distinctiveness of this monkey is poorly supported. We consider excubitor to be a synonym of Eastern Vervet C. p. centralis (Neumann, 1900).

We here recognize six subspecies of Vervet Chlorocebus pygerythrus: Northeastern Vervet C. p. arenaria (Heller, 1913), Eastern Vervet C. p. centralis (Neumann, 1900), Pemba Vervet C. p. nesiotes (Schwarz, 1926), Reddish-green Vervet C. p. rufoviridis (I. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, 1843), Omo Vervet C. p. zavattarii (de Beaux, 1943), and Southern Vervet C. p. pygerythrus (F. Cuvier, 1821). Recognizing hilgerti as a Grivet endemic to Ethiopia, and C. p. arenaria and C. p. centralis for East Africa, takes us back, in part, to the pre-2001 taxonomy for Chlorocebus (Pocock 1907; Elliot 1913; Schwarz 1926; Dandelot 1959, 1974; Hill 1966; Kingdon 1971; Napier 1981; Lernould 1988; Gippoliti 2018; Turner et al. 2019).

We here apply the taxonomic arrangement of Butynski and De Jong (2022) and De Jong and Butynski (2023).
